## Overall Goal of the Course

Students will learn scientific methods and tools that are essential for advanced
seminars at the university and relevant for advanced management activities. In
addition to core methodological skills, students learn to use modern AI tools
and the R programming language to perform applied research tasks in both
academic and business contexts.

## Learning Goals

At the end of the course, students will have acquired the following competences:

**Conceptual and argumentative competence:**

- Develop a command of basic logic, including the ability to identify arguments
  and deconstruct their logical structure and components, both in the writing of
  others and in one's own ideas.
- Cultivate the ability to grasp the main arguments and positions in a debate,
  and to neutrally describe and reflect on the arguments exchanged.

**Methodological competence:**

- Gain a broad overview of common research methods in the social sciences and
  business, including their strengths and weaknesses.
- Develop the ability to evaluate methodological approaches to specific research
  questions and select appropriate combinations of methods.
- Learn to effectively structure research projects and implement methodological
  approaches in the correct chronological order.

**Practical and computational skills:**

- Master the implementation of the covered research tools using the R
  programming language.
- Develop skills to produce professional, attractive, and reproducible research
  reports using Quarto.
- Gain project and knowledge management skills using modern tools such as Zotero
  for bibliographic management and Obsidian for note-taking.

## Structure and Basic Philosophy

The course consists of two parts: a **main lecture** and an **implementation
lab**. The lecture takes place every Monday and introduces the basics of the
various topics and tools. The implementation lab takes place every Friday and
combines face-to-face meetings with instructional videos; here you learn
hands-on how to implement the key tools using the programming language R.
It is therefore essential that you bring your laptop to each lab session.

## Course Information

### Prerequisites

This course does not require the completion of any other course in the IMS
Master's program, and we do not require prior knowledge of programming languages
or of any of the methods covered in this course (although it may be helpful).
We do, however, assume knowledge of some basic mathematical and statistical
concepts, which are listed in @sec-priorknowledge.

### Course Details

- **Main lecture:** Mondays, 11:30–13:00, Room MAD 024 (Madrid Building)
- **Implementation lab:** Fridays, 11:15–12:45, Room MAD 024 (Madrid Building).
  Note that the lab does *not* meet on site every week: several sessions are
  video labs that you work through on your own. Which Friday is which is
  indicated in the schedule below.
- **Lecture period:** 14 September – 11 December 2026 (no class in the week of
  12–16 October 2026)
- **Lecturers:** Claudius Gräbner-Radkowitsch (CGR) & Anna-Katharina Kothe (AKK)
- **Credits:** 5 ECTS ($\approx$ 150 h total workload; see @sec-workload)

### Course Resources

- **Course website:** <https://researchmethodology-fall26.netlify.app> — holds
  the material for both the lecture and the lab, including this description.
- **Moodle room:** [room 17920](https://elearning.uni-flensburg.de/moodle/course/view.php?id=17920),
  password `ResearchMethods26` — used for all official announcements, for the

## Workload {#sec-workload}

This course is worth 5 CP. Here is how the expected workload is distributed
among the various course activities:

| Activity | Time requirement |
|:--|:--|
| On-site lectures | $12 \cdot 1.5 = 18$ hours |
| On-site labs | $7 \cdot 1.5 = 10.5$ hours |
| Instructional videos | 10 hours |
| Expected self-study (including take-home examinations) | 111.5 hours |
| **Total workload** | **150 hours** |

We strongly recommend that you spread your study time fairly evenly throughout
the semester. It will save you time and effort if you study and practice
constantly, not just right before the exams.

## Evaluation and Assessment {#sec-evaluation}

The mark for this course is determined by the **final exam** at the end of the
semester. In order to be admitted to the final exam, you must pass two of the
three **take-home examinations** assigned during the semester. These take-home
examinations are graded on a pass/fail basis only and must be completed at home
on your own. **Each take-home examination is published on Moodle after the
lecture it belongs to**, and you have until the Sunday following that lecture to
submit it. The examination, together with an affidavit (*Eidesstattliche
Erklärung*), must be uploaded via Moodle. Late submissions are automatically
graded as fail.

The three take-home examinations are:

1. **Logic and argumentation** — published after the lecture of 5 October 2026
2. **Systematic literature review** — published after the lecture of
   9 November 2026
3. **Statistics** — published after the lecture of 16 November 2026

The final exam is a **120-minute open-book exam** that you take at the
university on your own laptop. You are free to bring any materials you wish and
to use all the tools you have learned about during the semester. However, it is
essential that you document any use of AI tools as explained during the course
and in the [AI disclosure template](https://researchmethodology-fall26.netlify.app/content/lecture/ai-disclosure/).
Failure to do so is considered cheating.

The content of the exam is as follows:

- 1/3 – 1/2: Multiple choice questions (via Moodle)
- 1/3 – 1/2: Open questions and technical applications (via Moodle)
- 1/3 – 1/2: R tasks (on your own computer, to be uploaded to Moodle)

## Required Prior Knowledge in Mathematics and Statistics {#sec-priorknowledge}

We assume knowledge of the basic mathematical and statistical areas described
below. If you do not have this knowledge, please make sure that you acquire it
as soon as possible; it is assumed in the take-home examination on statistics.
We strongly recommend that you review these concepts early in the semester and
ask questions via the Moodle forum. While we will do our best to help you with
this content, we are not responsible (and unable) to teach these topics in the
course itself.

- Fundamentals of probability theory (random variables, probability
  distributions, expected values)
- Fundamentals of calculus (derivatives, partial derivatives, basic
  optimization)
- Linear algebra essentials (vectors, matrices, matrix operations, determinants)
- Familiarity with statistical notation and terminology (indices, kinds of
  variables, scales of measurement)
- Familiarity with the concepts of variance, covariance, and correlation
  matrices
- Descriptive statistics (measures of central tendency, dispersion, and
  correlation)
- Basic inferential statistics (confidence intervals, hypothesis testing,
  p-values)
- Simple linear regression analysis (model assumptions, interpretation of
  coefficients)
- Understanding of statistical significance and effect sizes
- Basic understanding of sampling methods and their implications
- Ability to interpret common statistical output from software packages
- Understanding of model evaluation metrics ($R^2$, adjusted $R^2$, residual
  analysis)

A self-study recap of these concepts is available via the
[statistics recap track](https://euf-methodology-hub.netlify.app/tracks/statistics-recap)
of the EUF methodology hub.
